member.name: T:OpenIGI.Frontend.Settings.CVarBinding
member.summary: Builds a bound control for a console variable — a toggle, a slider or a dropdown, wired to the CVar both ways so the widget writes it live and an external change writes the widget back.

remarks.para: This is the heart of the settings screen: a row is a CVar rendered as the control its type calls for. A boolean is a toggle, an enum is a dropdown over its choices, and a numeric with both bounds is a slider; an unbounded number or free text has no gamepad-friendly control and returns none, so the screen shows it read-only. Writing the widget calls , whose event the game already listens to, so a change previews immediately.

The two directions are guarded against feeding back into each other: while the binding pushes a value one way it ignores the echo coming the other, so a preset that rewrites a dozen CVars updates their widgets without each update bouncing back through TrySetText.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Frontend.Settings.GraphicsMenu
member.summary: What the graphics page offers: the choices a player expects to find in a game's options, each standing in for however many of the renderer's own variables it takes to mean something.

remarks.para: The renderer exposes about a hundred graphics variables, and that is the right number for a renderer to expose. It is the wrong number to put in a menu — and, this page having learned it the hard way, it is the wrong number to put in a menu even behind a door marked Advanced. Somebody who wants light to bounce around a room is looking for "Global Illumination". They are not looking for a card atlas density, a distance-field voxel resolution, a relight amortisation window and a probe gather cadence, four values that are meaningless apart and have to move together to mean anything at all.

So there is one page and no second half. Every row here is a name for an idea the player already has, and the console remains what it always was: the place where every variable is reachable by anyone who knows what it is called. That is a better advanced interface than a list of a hundred sliders was, because it comes with completion, help text, a search and the ability to say what you mean.

The steps a group offers are exactly the values the four graphics presets use, which is what makes the page and the preset agree: a player on High finds every row reading High rather than Custom, and a row moved on its own drops the preset to Custom because the settings really are no longer any of the four. GraphicsMenuPresetAlignmentTests is what keeps that true — it was written because it had silently stopped being true, three rows having drifted from the table they claim to quote.

member.remarks: Every one of these is an r_ variable, so the old page collected them by prefix and put them among the quality settings. That is where the prefix stops being a good guide: whether the remastered HUD is drawn, whether spotted enemies are outlined, and whether rounds leave marks are choices about what the player is shown and what the game does, not about how well it is drawn. They belong beside the other gameplay and interface options, and a player looking for them looks there.

member.summary: Gets the archived graphics variables the page deliberately does not show, each with the reason.

remarks.para: A list rather than an absence, so that "not on the page" is a decision somebody made and can be argued with, rather than something that fell off. A new archived r_ variable has to be given a row or a line here; GraphicsMenuPresetAlignmentTests fails until it is.

Everything here is still reachable, and reachable the same way it always was: by name, from the console, with completion and its own help text. That is the advanced interface. What was removed was a menu page that listed all of them as sliders, which served nobody — a player could not tell which of "screen probe gather cadence" and "surface-cache relight amortisation" to move, and anyone who could already knew the console.

member.summary: Builds the control for a : one dropdown that writes every variable under it, and reads them back to say which step they currently are.

remarks.para: The counterpart to , which binds one control to one variable. Here one control stands over several, so the two directions are not symmetrical: choosing a step writes them all, while reading back has to recognise a step from what the variables happen to say — and sometimes none of them fits, because a variable has been set from the console on its own. That is what the extra Custom step is for. It is shown so the row can tell the truth, and disabled so it cannot be chosen: there is nothing for "make it custom" to write.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Frontend.Settings.QualityGroup
member.summary: A coarse quality choice on the graphics page: one caption the player understands over several variables they should not have to.

remarks.para: A group is a named point in the space its variables span. Choosing Shadow Quality: High writes six shadow variables at once, and the point of the type is that six is the number it takes for the answer to mean anything — a shadow resolution without its cascade count and its distance is not a setting, it is a third of one.

Nothing is hidden by this and nothing is duplicated in the settings file: every variable a group names is still itself, still archived under its own name, and still reachable from the console — which is where somebody goes who wants one of the six on its own.

It follows that a group has to be able to say "none of my steps": the moment one of those variables is set by hand the group is between its steps, and reporting the step it used to be on would be a lie the player can see through. That reading is 's, and is the same rule GraphicsPresetRegistry applies to the overall preset.

member.param: The row's caption.
What the choice does, for the tooltip and the footer.
The steps, in the order they are offered — quietest first.

member.summary: Changes made on a settings page that have not been applied: what the page's rows show and write, held back from the variables themselves until the player confirms them.
